subtitle: Write position descriptions and minimum qualifications that test what the work actually needs, so that essential functions, degree and experience requirements and language skills open the job to every qualified route and support accommodation from the start.
audience: For DHS and DSD supervisors, managers and leads who write or update position descriptions and request postings, and for the Human Resources partners and program staff who help draft and review them.

lessons.title: The position description comes before the posting
objectives: Distinguish a class specification, a position description and a job posting, and what each one does.
Recognize signs that a position description no longer matches the work at the moment a vacancy opens.
Write principal responsibilities as results the work must achieve rather than methods.
Plan who to involve before a posting is requested, including Human Resources and classification.
lessons.teaching:
Many problems that surface during selection began earlier, in documents written months or years before a vacancy opened. Three documents do different jobs. A class specification describes a classification that many positions share, and it connects those positions to a pay range. A position description describes one position: why it exists, its principal responsibilities and what the work requires. A job posting draws on both to tell applicants what the job is and which minimum and preferred qualifications they must show. Minnesota Management and Budget describes an accurate position description as an HR requirement used primarily for classification and vacancy filling, and notes that it also supports interview questions, realistic information for applicants, expectations and coaching. When these documents disagree, or when the position description no longer describes the real work, every later step inherits the problem.

Position descriptions drift. Duties are added during a staffing shortage and never removed, technology changes, program rules shift, or a description was copied from a similar position and never fitted to this one. Signs of drift include tasks no one has done in years, tools that no longer exist, responsibilities current staff carry that the description never mentions, and requirements that seem to describe the last person in the job rather than the work. A vacancy is the most important time to check, because once a posting goes out, every applicant is screened against what it says. Ask the people who do the work now, or who supervised it recently, what the position accomplishes, what takes most of the time and what would go wrong if a duty were not done.

Write principal responsibilities as results rather than methods. "Answers provider questions about service authorization rules accurately and within agreed timelines, by phone, email and meetings" states what must be achieved. "Spends most of the day on the phone at a desk" states one way of doing it, and it may exclude people who could achieve the same result another way. Results wording makes every later step easier. Minimum qualifications can be traced to responsibilities, interview questions can test them, and a conversation about accommodation can start from the outcome the job needs rather than the habits of the last person who held it. It also gives the employee who is eventually hired a clearer picture of what success looks like.

Role design is shared work, and the order matters. The supervisor knows the work. Human Resources knows classification, posting rules and how qualifications will be screened. The ADA coordinator can advise on how functions and physical demands are described, and labor relations can advise where a bargaining agreement affects duties or postings. Bring the draft to Human Resources before a posting is requested, so that classification questions are settled first; a changed position description can affect how the position is classified and paid. This course helps you bring a better draft. Formal decisions about classification, qualifications, accommodation and selection stay with the person or area responsible, such as Human Resources, Minnesota Management and Budget or the ADA coordinator.
lessons.keyPoint: The position description sets up every later step. Check it against the real work at each vacancy, write responsibilities as results, and bring it to Human Resources before a posting is requested.
lessons.example: Practice case: {{SUPERVISOR}} has a vacancy for a program consultant who supports lead agencies on waiver policy. The position description was last updated many years ago. It lists maintaining paper files and a fax log, and it says nothing about the virtual trainings and online guidance that the team now spends much of its time producing. Human Resources can post within the week if {{SUPERVISOR}} reuses the last posting as written.
lessons.question: What should {{SUPERVISOR}} do?
choices: Ask current staff what the role accomplishes, draft updated responsibilities, and review them with Human Resources before posting.
Reuse the last posting now so the vacancy fills quickly, and update the position description after the new hire learns the role.
Rewrite the description and the posting alone overnight, since the supervisor knows the work best and speed matters most here.
feedback: This checks the document against the real work and involves Human Resources before applicants are screened. A short delay usually costs less than screening every applicant against duties that no longer exist.
Applicants would be screened against outdated duties, and the people best suited to the current work may not apply or may be screened out. Updating the description afterward does not undo that.
Knowing the work is essential, but classification and posting rules are not the supervisor's alone. A rewrite without Human Resources can create classification problems and delay the hire further.
lessons.reflection: Privately think of a position description you know, your own or one you supervise, or use the practice case. Which parts describe the work as it is now, and which describe a past version of the job or a past person in it?
lessons.action: Pick one position you supervise or know well. Read its position description beside a week of the real work, mark duties that are missing, outdated or written as methods rather than results, and bring your notes to Human Resources before the next vacancy or review.

check.question: According to Minnesota Management and Budget, what is a position description primarily used for?
check.correct: Classification and filling vacancies, with further uses in supervision and coaching.
wrong: Setting each employee's pay directly, without review by Human Resources.
Recording an employee's accommodation and medical information for the file.
check.feedback: MMB describes an accurate position description as an HR requirement used primarily for classification and vacancy filling, and also as a tool for interviews, expectations and coaching. Pay follows classification through Human Resources and MMB, and accommodation information is kept confidential and separate.

lessons.title: Essential functions and how they connect to accommodation
objectives: Explain how the ADA and its regulations define essential and marginal functions and what evidence counts.
Explain why labeling too much or too little as essential causes problems later.
Describe a function by the outcome it requires rather than one method of doing it.
Involve the ADA coordinator when the way a function is described may affect accommodation.
lessons.teaching:
Under Title I of the Americans with Disabilities Act, a qualified individual is someone who, with or without reasonable accommodation, can perform the essential functions of the position they hold or want. The statute gives weight to the employer's judgment about which functions are essential, and it says that a written description prepared before advertising or interviewing applicants is considered evidence of those functions. That makes the position description more than an internal document. What it says about the work, and when it was written, can matter when an applicant or employee with a disability asks whether they can do the job with an accommodation.

The federal regulations define essential functions as the fundamental job duties of the position, not its marginal functions. A function may be essential because the position exists to perform it, because few other employees are available to share it, or because it is highly specialized and the person is hired for that expertise. Evidence includes the employer's judgment, written job descriptions prepared before advertising or interviewing, the time spent on the function, the consequences of not requiring it, the terms of a collective bargaining agreement, and the experience of past and current incumbents. A description that calls everything essential is weak evidence, because time records and incumbents' experience may show otherwise, and it can discourage qualified applicants who would need help only with a minor task.

Accuracy matters in both directions. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission's guidance on reasonable accommodation says an employer does not have to eliminate an essential function, and never has to reallocate essential functions as an accommodation, although it may choose to. Marginal functions are different: job restructuring can include reallocating marginal functions that an employee cannot perform because of a disability, or changing when or how a function is done. So listing a minor task as essential can exclude people unnecessarily, while leaving out a duty that truly is fundamental creates confusion later about what the job requires. The guidance was issued in 2002, before the ADA Amendments Act of 2008, so bring specific situations to the ADA coordinator or Human Resources.

Describe each function by what it must accomplish. "Visits provider sites across the region each month" states the need, while "must hold a valid driver's license" assumes one method that some people, including some disabled applicants, cannot use but could replace. "Explains complex policy clearly to providers and families" states the need, while "must speak clearly on the phone" assumes a method that could exclude a Deaf applicant who communicates through an interpreter or relay service. Physical demands copied from older templates, such as a lifting requirement in an office role, deserve the same test: does the position exist to do this, how often does it happen, and what happens if it is done another way? Outcome wording does not lower the standard. It keeps the standard on the result and leaves the method open for the accommodation process to work out with the person.
lessons.keyPoint: A description written before posting is evidence of a job's essential functions. Name the fundamental duties accurately, describe them by outcome rather than method, and let the accommodation process address how they are done.
lessons.example: Practice case: {{CASE_MANAGER}} is helping {{SUPERVISOR}} update the position description for a lead worker role in an office-based unit. The inherited template lists, as essential, lifting fifty pounds, driving a state vehicle, and answering the unit's phone line during all business hours. Current staff say the heaviest thing they carry is a box of training binders a few times a year, that site visits happen monthly and can be reached several ways, and that phone coverage rotates among five people.
lessons.question: How should they revise the essential functions?
choices: Keep all three listed as essential to be safe, and let any applicant who needs something different request an accommodation later.
Remove the lifting, travel and phone duties from the description entirely, so that no applicant is discouraged from applying.
Describe duties as outcomes, treat the lifting and phone coverage as marginal, and check travel wording with the ADA coordinator.
feedback: Overstating essential functions is not the safe choice. It weakens the description as evidence, discourages qualified applicants, and pushes people to disclose and request changes the job never needed.
Site visits are a real part of the work, so leaving them out would make the description inaccurate. The aim is accuracy about each duty, not silence about it.

This matches the description to the work. Occasional lifting and shared phone coverage look marginal, monthly travel is described by its purpose, and the ADA coordinator can advise on wording before it is final.
lessons.reflection: Privately consider a requirement in a job you know that describes a method rather than a result, or use the practice case. Who might be able to achieve the result another way, and what would they currently have to ask for?
lessons.action: Take one position description and, for each listed function, note why it is essential, how much time it takes and what would happen if it were done another way. Rewrite one method-based function as an outcome and review it with the ADA coordinator or Human Resources.

check.question: Under the ADA, why does it matter when a written job description was prepared?
check.correct: A description prepared before advertising or interviewing is considered evidence of essential functions.
wrong: A description written after hiring automatically replaces every earlier version as evidence.
Only descriptions updated within the past year count for accommodation purposes.
check.feedback: The statute says a written description prepared before advertising or interviewing applicants is considered evidence of essential functions. It is one form of evidence among several, alongside time spent, consequences and incumbents' experience. There is no one-year rule.

lessons.title: Minimum qualifications: degrees, equivalent experience and licenses
objectives: Explain what a minimum qualification does in screening and why it must be tied to a responsibility.
Apply current state guidance on when a degree may be required and how alternative pathways work.
Separate day-one requirements from trainable skills that belong in preferred qualifications.
Write a qualification that names the skill and the range of experience that can show it.
lessons.teaching:
A minimum qualification is a gate. Minnesota Management and Budget's guidance to agencies notes that applicants who do not pass the initial minimum qualification screening are not considered further, which is why qualifications should be targeted, specific and clearly tied to the job's responsibilities. A preferred qualification works differently: it helps distinguish among people who already meet the minimum. Each minimum qualification therefore deserves a direct question. Which responsibility in the position description does it support, and would a person without it be unable to do that work on the first day? If the honest answer is that the skill can be learned on the job, MMB's guidance says it can be a preferred qualification but should not be a minimum one.

Degrees are the clearest example. Executive Order 23-14, signed on October 30, 2023, directed MMB to update hiring guidance so that a degree is used as a minimum qualification only where state or federal licensure or certification requires it, where law requires it, or in rare cases where the required skills or knowledge can be obtained only through a degree program. It also said agencies shall provide alternative pathways to qualification whenever possible. MMB's February 2024 guidance repeats that, outside those cases, a degree cannot be the only way to qualify. Executive orders can change. Under the order's own terms and Minnesota law, an executive order expires 90 days after the governor who issued it leaves office unless it is rescinded or ends earlier, so confirm with Human Resources which order and guidance apply when you draft a posting.

Alternative pathways work best when the qualification names the skill first. "Bachelor's degree in social work" names a credential. "Experience applying eligibility or service rules to individual situations and explaining decisions in writing" names the skill and lets more routes count, which fits MMB's note that relevant experience may come from work, internships, fellowships or volunteering. Years of experience deserve the same scrutiny. A requirement of five years at a state agency may stand in for knowing how public programs work, which someone may have learned at a county, a Tribal agency, a provider or as a family member navigating services. Licenses and certifications follow the same rule: MMB's guidance says only those necessary to perform the duties may be required, and others may only be preferred.

Consistency matters across a team. MMB's guidance notes that positions at the same level need not have identical qualifications but should require comparable education and experience. If one unit requires a master's degree for work that another unit fills through experience, ask why. Also make sure the qualifications can be screened fairly and the same way for everyone. An applicant should be able to see from the posting what counts, and a screener should be able to tell from an application whether it was shown. Draft qualifications with that screening in mind, and ask Human Resources how equivalencies will be applied before the posting goes out, not after applications arrive.
lessons.keyPoint: A minimum qualification screens people out, so tie each one to a day-one responsibility, name the skill before the credential, let experience from several settings count, and confirm current degree guidance with Human Resources.
lessons.example: Practice case: {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} is drafting a posting for a policy analyst who will write guidance on service changes. The draft minimum qualifications require a master's degree in public policy and five years of experience at a state agency. The role involves no license. A similar analyst position at the same level in another unit requires a bachelor's degree or equivalent experience and two years of policy work.
lessons.question: What should {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} change before sending the draft to Human Resources?
choices: Keep the master's degree as a minimum, but add a note that strong experience may also be considered during the interviews.
Name the analysis and writing skills needed, let several kinds of experience show them, and compare with the similar position.
Remove all education and experience requirements from the posting, so that the screening cannot exclude any applicant at all.
feedback: Applicants without the degree would be screened out before any interview, so the note about experience would never be reached. The degree would still be the only way in.
This ties the gate to the work, opens alternative pathways as current guidance expects, and checks consistency with a comparable position before Human Resources reviews the draft.
Minimum qualifications have a real purpose. The work needs analysis and writing skills at a set level, and screening for them fairly is better than screening for nothing.
lessons.reflection: Privately think about your own path into your current role, or use the practice case. Which of your skills came from places a typical posting would not have counted, and what wording would have recognized them?
lessons.action: For one posting you expect to draft or review, list each minimum qualification beside the responsibility it supports. Mark any skill that could be learned on the job, any credential that stands in for a skill and any experience tied to a single setting, then bring a revised draft to Human Resources.

check.question: Under current state hiring guidance, when may a degree be the only way to meet a minimum qualification?
check.correct: When licensure, certification or law requires it, or only a degree provides the skill.
wrong: Whenever the hiring supervisor believes a degree signals stronger writing and analysis ability.
Whenever the last person who held the position had earned that same degree.
check.feedback: Executive Order 23-14 and MMB's 2024 guidance limit degree-only requirements to licensure, certification, legal requirements and rare cases where only a degree program provides the skill, and they call for alternative pathways whenever possible. Confirm with Human Resources that this guidance still applies.

lessons.title: Language skills as a qualification, and who reviews the design
objectives: Decide when a language skill, including American Sign Language, is a genuine job requirement and at what level.
Distinguish a language requirement from assumptions about national origin, accent or who people prefer.
Describe how a language qualification should be verified the same way for every applicant.
Bring a complete role design to the right reviewers, in the right order, before a posting is requested.
lessons.teaching:
Many DSD positions work with people and partners who use languages other than English, including American Sign Language. When the work genuinely requires communicating in another language, that skill can be a legitimate qualification and may be among the most important ones. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission's guidance on national origin discrimination says that requiring fluency in a language other than English is permissible only if it is required for the effective performance of the position, and that employers may assign work based on an employee's ability to speak another language. The guidance applies a parallel test to English: a fluency or proficiency requirement is permissible only if required for effective performance, and requiring more fluency than a position needs may violate Title VII. The guidance dates from 2016 and does not itself have the force of law, so confirm current requirements with Human Resources.

The design questions are about the work. Which responsibilities require the language, how often, and for what tasks? Explaining a notice in conversation, leading a meeting and translating written material are different skills at different levels. A qualification such as "able to explain service options and answer questions in Somali in conversation with families" is specific and can be tested. A vague phrase like "bilingual preferred" leaves screeners guessing, and "excellent verbal communication" may screen out people who communicate effectively through an interpreter or with an accent. The EEOC guidance distinguishes a merely discernible accent from one that materially interferes with the spoken communication a job requires, and it says employers may not rely on coworker, customer or client preference to justify an accent-based decision.

Verification has to be the same for everyone. If a language skill is a qualification, decide with Human Resources how it will be assessed, and assess every applicant who claims it the same way. Do not infer language ability from a name, a background or where someone grew up, and do not assume that someone from a community speaks its languages or wants to serve as the unit's interpreter. A position that requires a language skill may also raise questions about classification, pay or how language work is counted in a workload; those belong with Human Resources and labor relations, not in a supervisor's posting draft. Keep a stated, tested language skill separate from choosing a person because of assumptions about whom families would prefer.

Then bring the whole design together before a posting is requested. Start with the position description checked against the real work. Mark essential and marginal functions and describe them by outcome. Draft minimum and preferred qualifications that trace to responsibilities, with alternative pathways where guidance calls for them and any language requirement stated at a level that can be tested. Review the draft with Human Resources, including classification; with the ADA coordinator if functions or physical demands might affect accommodation; and with labor relations if a bargaining agreement may affect duties or the posting. Date the final version. Changing the criteria after applications arrive, without Human Resources, undermines fairness and weakens the description as evidence of what the job requires.
lessons.keyPoint: Treat a language as a skill the work requires, at a stated level, verified the same way for everyone. Then bring the full role design to Human Resources, classification, the ADA coordinator and labor relations before posting.
lessons.example: Practice case: {{COMMUNITY_PARTNER}}, from a county that refers many Somali-speaking families to a DSD program, tells {{SUPERVISOR}} that the next hire should be Somali. {{SUPERVISOR}} is drafting the posting for a role that answers families' questions about service options. About a third of the role's calls are with Somali-speaking families, and interpreter scheduling now adds days to many responses.
lessons.question: How should {{SUPERVISOR}} handle the language need in the posting?
choices: Add a preference for candidates from the Somali community, since they are most likely to understand what families need.
State conversational Somali for explaining service options as a qualification, and agree with Human Resources how to test it.
Leave language out of the posting and keep using interpreters, since any language requirement could look like national origin bias.
feedback: Preferring people from a community is a choice based on national origin, not a skill. It also assumes that everyone from that community speaks the language and that families prefer them.
This turns the partner's concern into a job-related skill at a stated level, tested the same way for every applicant, and leaves classification and pay questions with Human Resources.
A language skill tied to a third of the work can be a legitimate qualification. Leaving it out keeps families waiting, and interpreters remain available for other languages and situations.
lessons.reflection: Privately consider a time a language or communication requirement at work seemed to measure something other than the work, or use the practice case. What would a requirement tied to the actual task have said?
lessons.action: Use the job aid to review one role design from start to finish: the position description, essential and marginal functions, minimum and preferred qualifications, and any language requirement. Note who must review each part, and schedule the Human Resources review before a posting is requested.

check.question: Which language qualification best fits the EEOC's national origin guidance?
check.correct: Explains service options in Hmong in conversation, assessed the same way for all.
wrong: Native speaker of Hmong preferred, to match the families the program serves most.
Must speak English without any accent, to ensure that all phone calls are clear.
check.feedback: A qualification should name the task and level the work needs and be verified consistently. Native-speaker status points to origin rather than skill, and an accent is not a barrier unless it materially interferes with the communication the job requires.

cards.back: A class specification describes a classification that many positions share. A position description describes one position's purpose, responsibilities and requirements.
A fundamental duty of the position, not a marginal one. Evidence includes why the position exists, time spent, consequences of not doing it and incumbents' experience.
Under the ADA, a written job description prepared before advertising or interviewing applicants is considered evidence of the job's essential functions.
Describe what a duty must achieve, such as reaching provider sites or explaining policy clearly, rather than one method of doing it.
A gate. Applicants who do not meet it are not considered further, so it must be tied to a responsibility a person must perform on day one.
A way to qualify without a degree, such as experience from work, internships, fellowships or volunteering, unless licensure, law or a rare skill need requires the degree.
A language skill required for effective performance of the position, stated at a level and tested the same way for every applicant.

aid.heading: Check the position description
items: Compare it with a week of the real work and talk with the people who do it now.
Remove outdated tasks and add responsibilities current staff actually carry.
Write principal responsibilities as results rather than methods.
Bring the draft to Human Resources before requesting a posting.

aid.heading: Mark essential functions
items: For each function, note why it is essential, the time it takes and what happens if it is done another way.
Treat occasional or shareable tasks as marginal.
Replace method wording with outcome wording.
Ask the ADA coordinator about physical demands and travel wording.

aid.heading: Set minimum qualifications
items: Trace each one to a responsibility a person must perform on day one.
Move trainable skills, and licenses the duties do not need, to preferred qualifications.
Name the skill before any credential and let several kinds of experience count.
Confirm current degree guidance and how equivalencies will be applied with Human Resources.

aid.heading: State language needs
items: Name the task, the language and the level the work requires.
Agree with Human Resources how the skill will be assessed for every applicant.
Never infer language ability or preference from a name or background.
Take classification, pay and workload questions to Human Resources and labor relations.

sources.title: ADA.gov — Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, as amended
sources.note: Supports the definition of a qualified individual, the weight given to the employer's judgment and to a written description prepared before advertising or interviewing (42 U.S.C. 12111(8)), and the job-related standard for qualification standards that screen out people with disabilities (lesson 2). Applying it to a specific position is a question for the ADA coordinator.

sources.title: Title 29 Code of Federal Regulations, section 1630.2 — Definitions (Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School)
sources.note: Supports the definition of essential and marginal functions, the reasons a function may be essential and the list of evidence in paragraph (n) (lesson 2). A secondary reproduction; confirm the current text on eCFR.

sources.title: U.S. EEOC — Enforcement Guidance on Reasonable Accommodation and Undue Hardship under the ADA
sources.note: Supports the statements that an employer need not eliminate or reallocate essential functions and that restructuring can include reallocating marginal functions (lesson 2). Issued in 2002, before the ADA Amendments Act of 2008; it is agency guidance, not law.

sources.title: Executive Order 23-14: Improving Access to State Employment (Minnesota Legislative Reference Library)
sources.note: Supports the limits on degree requirements, the call for alternative pathways and the order's expiration terms (lesson 3). Signed October 30, 2023; confirm with Human Resources that it remains in effect.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Top 10 Tips for Setting and Assessing Minimum Qualifications (February 14, 2024)
sources.note: Supports the guidance that minimum qualifications screen applicants out, that trainable skills belong in preferred qualifications, that a degree cannot be the only route outside the order's exceptions, and that experience may come from several settings (lesson 3). A bulletin pointing to a fuller MMB guide; agency procedures may add detail.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Position Descriptions
sources.note: Supports the description of a position description as an HR requirement used primarily for classification and vacancy filling, with uses in interviews, expectations and coaching (lesson 1). It does not address essential functions or minimum qualifications.

sources.title: U.S. EEOC — Enforcement Guidance on National Origin Discrimination (November 18, 2016)
sources.note: Supports the standards for English fluency, fluency in other languages and accent, and the statement that customer or client preference does not justify an accent-based decision (lesson 4). Agency guidance without the force of law; check its current status.
